title: the sages
hook: who were the old people living in the forest, and why had they gone there at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sages, part one. In the hermitages of Dandaka they welcomed Rama and said: city or forest, you are our king. Protect us. Did you show up for someone who relies on you? Day five hundred fifty-one.

Take a retired couple: the kids are grown, there are grandchildren, the house is paid off. Today they might downsize, or travel. The old law books describe another option: go to the forest. Leave the house to your children, take a few things, and spend the rest of your life on prayer and simple living. Some readers picture the people who greeted Rama in that ring of huts this way.
screen: `THE KIDS ARE GROWN.` → `ANOTHER OPTION: THE FOREST.` → `WHO GREETED RAMA.`

segments.voice: Hindu law books describe life in four stages, called ashramas. First the student, learning. Then the householder, raising a family and working. Third comes vanaprastha, literally the forest dweller. The Laws of Manu say a householder may take this step when he sees his skin wrinkled, his hair gray, and his children's children born. He can go with his wife or alone, eat what grows wild, keep the sacred fires, and study. And for some, a fourth stage: complete renunciation. It was an ideal, and not everyone lived it, then or now. But it gave the forest a shape. It wasn't only wilderness. It was where people went to finish their lives well. Among them were the great sages. Two words come up again and again. A rishi is a seer, one to whom sacred hymns were revealed. A muni is often explained as the silent one, someone whose practice includes holding back speech. What they all share is tapas. The word means heat, and it's used for the discipline of austerity: fasting, standing in the sun, sitting through the cold. In the epics, tapas builds real power. A sage's blessing or curse can change a king's fate. Which makes their request to Rama even more striking. These people aren't helpless. They've simply chosen not to fight. And here comes Rama, dressed exactly like them in bark and matted hair, but carrying a bow.
screen: `FOUR STAGES OF LIFE.` · `VANAPRASTHA: THE FOREST DWELLER.` · `RISHI AND MUNI.` · `TAPAS: THE HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `DRESSED LIKE THEM, WITH A BOW.`

segments.voice: Try a small taste of the muni's practice: silence. For this sit, don't speak, not even in your head if you can help it. When words start up inside, a list, a reply to a message, a comment, notice them and let them trail off unfinished. Come back to the sound of your breathing. Two minutes without having to say anything. The bell holds the time.
The sages. Forest dwellers, seers and silent ones, living by tapas, the heat of discipline, who chose not to fight.
Your line: tapas, the heat of discipline. Today, give one conversation a moment of silence before you answer. Day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: The four stages of life remain an ideal in Hindu teaching; some older Hindus today take on a simpler, more prayerful life after their working years, though few literally move to the forest.

fork.setup: you're a householder in the world of the old law books. your hair is gray and your grandchildren are born. what do the books describe next?
options: go to the forest as a vanaprastha.
fork.reveal: the Laws of Manu describe this as the time to leave for the forest, with your wife or alone.

original.note: Sanskrit tapas: heat, glow; used for austerity, the discipline that, in the epics, gives sages power.

trapdoor: what you thought: the forest sages are hermits who ran away from life.
what it means: some may be in the third stage of life, finishing it in prayer.
what a scholar hears: Manusmriti 6 sets out the vanaprastha stage; in the epics, tapas is a real force that can bless or curse.

notes: Outline gives no beat for this day; built from the camp theme as background on the forest sages.
